name: cross_vs_comma
left: SELECT a.id, b.id AS bid FROM a CROSS JOIN b
right: SELECT a.id, b.id AS bid FROM a, b
why: A comma join is a cross join.

name: cross_vs_inner_on_true
left: SELECT a.id, b.id AS bid FROM a CROSS JOIN b
right: SELECT a.id, b.id AS bid FROM a JOIN b ON TRUE
why: An inner join on TRUE keeps every pair, as a cross join does.

name: comma_where_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a, b WHERE a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
why: Filtering the cross product by the join condition is the inner join.

name: inner_vs_left_is_not_null_join_col
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NOT NULL
why: b.k IS NOT NULL drops exactly the null-extended rows: a matched row has b.k = a.k, so b.k is not NULL.

name: inner_vs_left_where_filter
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
why: b.y > 0 is never TRUE on a null-extended row, so WHERE removes what the outer join adds.

name: inner_on_filter_vs_left_where
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
why: Same rows: the inner join keeps matches with b.y > 0, the outer join's extra rows fail b.y > 0.

name: inner_vs_left_is_not_null_key
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.id IS NOT NULL
why: b.id is NOT NULL in every stored row, so b.id IS NOT NULL keeps exactly the matched rows.

name: inner_vs_left_where_eq_repeat
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = b.k
why: Repeating the join condition in WHERE rejects the null-extended rows.

name: comma_vs_left_where
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a, b WHERE a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NOT NULL
why: Comma join with a join filter is the inner join; the outer join minus null-extended rows is too.

name: inner_vs_left_then_inner_reads_b
left: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = b.id
why: The later inner join compares c.k = b.id, which is never TRUE when b is null-extended.

name: ne_inner_chain_vs_left_chain_where_nullable
left: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k LEFT JOIN c ON c.k = b.id WHERE c.z > 0 OR c.z <= 0
why: c.z > 0 OR c.z <= 0 also drops matched rows whose c.z is NULL, which the inner chain keeps.

name: left_chain_rejected_transitively
left: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = b.id WHERE c.z > 0
right: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k LEFT JOIN c ON c.k = b.id WHERE c.z > 0
why: c.z > 0 rejects null-extended c rows; c can only match when b matched (c.k = b.id), so both outer joins are inner.

name: cross_vs_left_on_true_marker
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a CROSS JOIN b
right: SELECT a.id, t.y FROM a LEFT JOIN (SELECT y, 1 AS m FROM b) AS t ON TRUE WHERE t.m IS NOT NULL
why: The constant column m is never NULL in a real row, so m IS NOT NULL keeps the cross product and drops the one null-extended row an empty b adds.

name: cross_vs_left_on_true_not_null_key
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a CROSS JOIN b
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON TRUE WHERE b.id IS NOT NULL
why: b.id is NOT NULL, so b.id IS NOT NULL removes the null-extended row an empty b would add.

name: cross_scalar_agg_vs_left_on_true
left: SELECT a.id, t.n FROM a CROSS JOIN (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM b) AS t
right: SELECT a.id, t.n FROM a LEFT JOIN (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM b) AS t ON TRUE
why: An aggregate without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so the right side is never empty.

name: fk_inner_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
why: a.k is NOT NULL and references b.id, so every a row has a match.

name: right_vs_left_mirrored
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON a.k = b.k
why: a RIGHT JOIN b is b LEFT JOIN a with the same condition.

name: right_outer_vs_left_mirrored
left: SELECT a.x, b.y FROM a RIGHT OUTER JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND a.x > 1
right: SELECT a.x, b.y FROM b LEFT OUTER JOIN a ON a.k = b.k AND a.x > 1
why: Mirroring keeps the whole ON condition, including the test on the null-extended side.

name: right_where_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0
why: a.x > 0 rejects the rows where a is null-extended.

name: full_where_left_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0
why: a.x > 0 rejects the FULL JOIN rows whose a side is NULL, leaving a LEFT JOIN.

name: full_where_right_vs_left_mirrored
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
why: b.y > 0 rejects the rows whose b side is NULL, leaving b LEFT JOIN a.

name: full_where_both_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0 AND b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0 AND b.y > 0
why: Tests on both sides reject both kinds of null-extended row.

name: full_is_not_null_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k IS NOT NULL
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k IS NOT NULL
why: a.k IS NOT NULL rejects rows whose a side is NULL; matched rows have a.k = b.k, so it keeps all of them.

name: anti_left_is_null_vs_not_exists
left: SELECT a.id, a.x FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id, a.x FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k)
why: b.k IS NULL holds exactly on null-extended rows (a match has b.k = a.k, not NULL), one per unmatched a row.

name: anti_left_is_null_key_vs_not_exists
left: SELECT a.id, a.x FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.id IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id, a.x FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k)
why: b.id is NOT NULL, so b.id IS NULL holds exactly on the null-extended rows.

name: anti_left_is_null_extra_on_vs_not_exists
left: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.y > 0 WHERE b.k IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k AND b.y > 0)
why: The extra ON test belongs to the match, so it moves into the NOT EXISTS.

name: anti_left_is_null_vs_not_in_notnull
left: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE a.k NOT IN (SELECT k FROM b)
why: With a.k and b.k NOT NULL, NOT IN is NOT EXISTS.

name: semi_left_distinct_vs_exists
left: SELECT DISTINCT a.id, a.x FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NOT NULL
right: SELECT DISTINCT a.id, a.x FROM a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k)
why: DISTINCT removes the duplicates that several matches create.

name: semi_left_unique_vs_exists
left: SELECT a.id, a.x FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id WHERE b.id IS NOT NULL
right: SELECT a.id, a.x FROM a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.id = a.k)
why: b.id is a key, so each a row matches at most once.

name: semi_left_vs_in_distinct
left: SELECT DISTINCT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NOT NULL
right: SELECT DISTINCT a.id FROM a WHERE a.k IN (SELECT k FROM b)
why: DISTINCT over a semi join written as an outer join is IN.

name: count_having_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id
why: COUNT(b.k) ignores null-extended rows, and HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0 drops groups with no match.

name: ne_cross_vs_left_on_true
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a CROSS JOIN b
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON TRUE
why: An empty b gives no row in the cross join and one null-extended row per a row in the LEFT JOIN.

name: ne_inner_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
why: An a row without a match appears only in the LEFT JOIN.

name: ne_inner_vs_left_is_not_null_nullable
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y IS NOT NULL
why: b.y can be NULL in a matched row, which the WHERE drops.

name: ne_on_filter_vs_where_filter_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
why: A filter on the null-extended side in ON keeps unmatched a rows; in WHERE it drops them.

name: ne_left_filter_on_preserved_side
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND a.x > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0
why: A test on a in ON keeps the a row (null-extended); in WHERE it drops it.

name: ne_left_or_filter_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0 OR a.x > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0 OR a.x > 0
why: a.x > 0 can keep a null-extended row.

name: ne_left_coalesce_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE COALESCE(b.y, 0) = 0
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE COALESCE(b.y, 0) = 0
why: COALESCE(b.y, 0) = 0 is TRUE on a null-extended row.

name: ne_right_not_mirrored
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
why: RIGHT JOIN keeps unmatched b rows, LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched a rows.

name: ne_full_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
why: FULL JOIN also keeps unmatched b rows.

name: ne_full_or_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0 OR b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x > 0 OR b.y > 0
why: b.y > 0 can keep an unmatched b row.

name: ne_anti_nullable_col_vs_not_exists
left: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k)
why: b.y IS NULL also holds on matched rows whose b.y is NULL.

name: ne_anti_vs_not_in_nullable
left: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE a.k NOT IN (SELECT k FROM b)
why: NOT IN is never TRUE when b.k has a NULL or a.k is NULL.

name: ne_semi_left_bag_vs_exists
left: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NOT NULL
right: SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k)
why: Without DISTINCT, an a row with two matches appears twice.

name: ne_anti_extra_on_moved_to_where
left: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k IS NULL AND b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.k = a.k AND b.y > 0)
why: b.y > 0 in WHERE is never TRUE on the null-extended row the anti join keeps.

name: ne_fk_nullable_inner_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
why: Without a declared foreign key, an a row can lack a parent.

name: ne_count_star_having_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(*) > 0
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id
why: COUNT(*) counts the null-extended row, so the HAVING keeps unmatched a rows.

name: ne_cross_agg_grouped_vs_left_on_true
left: SELECT a.id, t.n FROM a CROSS JOIN (SELECT k, COUNT(*) AS n FROM b GROUP BY k) AS t
right: SELECT a.id, t.n FROM a LEFT JOIN (SELECT k, COUNT(*) AS n FROM b GROUP BY k) AS t ON TRUE
why: A grouped aggregate over an empty b returns no row.

name: inner_vs_left_in_subquery
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y IN (SELECT z FROM c)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y IN (SELECT z FROM c)
why: NULL IN (subquery) is NULL or FALSE, never TRUE, so the WHERE rejects null-extended rows.

name: inner_vs_left_exists_correlated
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y)
why: With b.y NULL, c.k = b.y is never TRUE, so EXISTS is FALSE on null-extended rows.

name: inner_vs_left_mod
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE MOD(b.y, 2) = 0
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE MOD(b.y, 2) = 0
why: MOD(NULL, 2) is NULL.

name: inner_vs_left_concat
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE CONCAT(CAST(b.y AS STRING), 'x') = '1x'
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE CONCAT(CAST(b.y AS STRING), 'x') = '1x'
why: CONCAT returns NULL when an argument is NULL (BigQuery).

name: inner_vs_left_greatest_unq
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y + a.x > 3
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y + a.x > 3
why: b.y + a.x is NULL on a null-extended row.

name: full_upper_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x + 1 > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x + 1 > 0
why: a.x + 1 > 0 rejects rows whose a side is NULL.

name: full_in_list_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x IN (1, 2)
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x IN (1, 2)
why: a.x IN (1, 2) rejects rows whose a side is NULL.

name: full_chain_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y, c.z FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = a.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y, c.z FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = a.id
why: The later inner join's c.k = a.id rejects rows whose a side is NULL.

name: full_or_both_sides_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x = b.y
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x = b.y
why: a.x = b.y rejects both kinds of null-extended row.

name: right_on_join_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a RIGHT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = a.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = a.id
why: The later inner join's c.k = a.id rejects rows whose a side is NULL.

name: left_then_inner_on_rejects
left: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = b.id AND c.z > b.y
right: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = b.id AND c.z > b.y
why: c.k = b.id in the next inner join rejects null-extended b rows.

name: sum_having_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.x, SUM(b.y) AS s FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING SUM(b.y) > 10
right: SELECT a.x, SUM(b.y) AS s FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING SUM(b.y) > 10
why: SUM(b.y) ignores null-extended rows and is NULL over none, so SUM(b.y) > 10 drops groups with no match.

name: count_having_ge1_vs_inner_nonkey
left: SELECT a.x, COUNT(b.id) AS n, MAX(b.y) AS m FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING COUNT(b.id) >= 1
right: SELECT a.x, COUNT(b.id) AS n, MAX(b.y) AS m FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x
why: Groups by a non-key: null-extended rows add nothing to COUNT(b.id) or MAX(b.y), and groups with no match fail the HAVING.

name: ne_count_left_vs_inner_no_having
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id
why: The LEFT JOIN reports unmatched a rows with a count of 0.

name: ne_having_mixed_agg
left: SELECT a.x, SUM(a.id) AS s FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0
right: SELECT a.x, SUM(a.id) AS s FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x
why: SUM(a.id) also adds the a rows that had no match, inside groups that survive.

name: ne_having_count_eq0
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(b.k) < 5
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(b.k) < 5
why: COUNT(b.k) < 5 keeps groups with no match.

name: ne_not_in_subquery_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y NOT IN (SELECT z FROM c)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y NOT IN (SELECT z FROM c)
why: NULL NOT IN (empty set) is TRUE.

name: ne_not_exists_correlated_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y)
why: NOT EXISTS is TRUE on a null-extended row.

name: ne_exists_or_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y OR c.z = a.x)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y OR c.z = a.x)
why: c.z = a.x can make EXISTS TRUE on a null-extended row.

name: ne_fk_after_left_join
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM c LEFT JOIN a ON a.id = c.k JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM c LEFT JOIN a ON a.id = c.k LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
why: a is null-extended by the earlier LEFT JOIN, so a.k can be NULL there despite the declaration.

name: fk_inner_vs_left_after_inner
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM c JOIN a ON a.id = c.k JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM c JOIN a ON a.id = c.k LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
why: a comes in through an inner join, so its rows are real and a.k always has a parent.

name: ne_fk_extra_on_filter
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.id AND b.y > 0
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id AND b.y > 0
why: The extra ON test can fail for the parent row.

name: ne_fk_wrong_parent_col
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
why: The foreign key is on b.id, not b.k.

name: right_nested_vs_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y, c.z FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k RIGHT JOIN c ON c.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y, c.z FROM c LEFT JOIN (a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k) ON c.k = b.id
why: a JOIN b RIGHT JOIN c keeps every c row and attaches the (a, b) pairs that match it: c LEFT JOIN (a JOIN b).

name: ne_fk_declared_but_nullable
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.id
why: a.k is declared a foreign key but may be NULL, and NULL has no parent.

name: ne_fk_parent_first
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM b JOIN a ON a.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON a.k = b.id
why: The foreign key says every a row has a b row, not that every b row has an a row.

name: fk_inner_vs_left_reversed_on
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON b.id = a.k
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.id = a.k
why: The same foreign-key join with the equality written the other way round.

name: ne_having_or_group_key
left: SELECT a.x, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0 OR a.x > 1
right: SELECT a.x, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0 OR a.x > 1
why: a.x > 1 can keep a group with no match.

name: ne_having_coalesce_agg
left: SELECT a.id, SUM(COALESCE(b.y, 1)) AS s FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING SUM(COALESCE(b.y, 1)) > 0
right: SELECT a.id, SUM(COALESCE(b.y, 1)) AS s FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING SUM(COALESCE(b.y, 1)) > 0
why: COALESCE(b.y, 1) counts null-extended rows as 1.

name: ne_having_is_null
left: SELECT a.id, MAX(b.y) AS m FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING MAX(b.y) IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id, MAX(b.y) AS m FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING MAX(b.y) IS NULL
why: MAX(b.y) IS NULL holds for groups with no match.

name: having_global_count_vs_inner
left: SELECT COUNT(b.k) AS n, MAX(b.y) AS m FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0
right: SELECT COUNT(b.k) AS n, MAX(b.y) AS m FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k HAVING COUNT(b.k) > 0
why: One group either way; null-extended rows add nothing to COUNT(b.k) or MAX(b.y).

name: having_count_distinct_vs_inner
left: SELECT a.x, COUNT(DISTINCT b.y) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING SUM(b.y) + COUNT(b.k) > 2
right: SELECT a.x, COUNT(DISTINCT b.y) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.x HAVING SUM(b.y) + COUNT(b.k) > 2
why: COUNT(DISTINCT b.y), SUM and COUNT all skip null-extended rows; SUM(b.y) + COUNT(b.k) > 2 is NULL over no match.

name: ne_having_count_ge0
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(b.k) >= 0
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(b.k) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(b.k) >= 0
why: COUNT(b.k) >= 0 keeps groups with no match.

name: ne_having_second_left_join
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(c.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k LEFT JOIN c ON c.k = a.x GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(c.k) > 0
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(c.k) AS n FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = a.x GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(c.k) > 0
why: Only the join to c is rejected; an a row without a b match but with a c match differs.

name: having_second_left_join
left: SELECT a.id, COUNT(c.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k LEFT JOIN c ON c.k = a.x GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(c.k) > 0
right: SELECT a.id, COUNT(c.k) AS n FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k JOIN c ON c.k = a.x GROUP BY a.id HAVING COUNT(c.k) > 0
why: COUNT(c.k) > 0 makes the join to c inner; the join to b stays outer.

name: nested_left_group_vs_derived
left: SELECT a.id, c.z FROM c LEFT JOIN (a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k) ON c.k = a.id
right: SELECT t.id, c.z FROM c LEFT JOIN (SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k) AS t ON c.k = t.id
why: A parenthesized join group reads like a derived table of its columns.

name: ne_nested_group_vs_flat_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y, c.z FROM c LEFT JOIN (a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k) ON c.k = b.id
right: SELECT a.id, b.y, c.z FROM c LEFT JOIN b ON c.k = b.id LEFT JOIN a ON a.k = b.k
why: The flat form keeps a b match even when no a row matches it.

name: ne_exists_shadowed_alias
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c AS b WHERE b.k = a.x)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM c AS b WHERE b.k = a.x)
why: Inside the subquery b names c, so the EXISTS says nothing about the outer b.

name: ne_exists_aggregate
left: SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y)
right: SELECT a.id FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE EXISTS (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM c WHERE c.k = b.y)
why: An aggregate subquery always returns a row, so EXISTS is TRUE.

name: eqi_where_key_into_on
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 2
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k = 2 WHERE a.k = 2
why: A kept a row has a.k = 2, so its matches have b.k = 2; the other a rows are filtered either way.

name: eqi_on_const_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND a.k = 2
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k = 2
why: Inside the ON, a.k = b.k makes a test on a.k the same test on b.k.

name: eqi_on_chain
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k = b.y
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND a.k = b.y
why: Inside the ON, a.k = b.k lets b.k = b.y read as a.k = b.y.

name: eqi_on_range_both
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND a.k > 1
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k > 1
why: Inside the ON, a.k = b.k makes a.k > 1 the same as b.k > 1.

name: eqi_select_swap
left: SELECT a.k, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
right: SELECT b.k, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.y > 0
why: b.y > 0 makes the join inner, where a.k = b.k on every row.

name: eqi_full_where_both
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a FULL JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 2 AND b.k = 2
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 2
why: Tests on both sides make the FULL JOIN inner; a.k = 2 then gives b.k = 2.

name: eqi_derived_filter
left: SELECT t.id, t.y FROM (SELECT a.id, a.k, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k) AS t WHERE t.k = 1
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN (SELECT * FROM b WHERE k = 1) AS b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 1
why: The filter on t.k is a.k = 1, which carries through the ON to b.k = 1.

name: ne_eqi_where_right_into_left
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE b.k = 2 OR b.k IS NULL
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 2
why: b.k IS NULL keeps every unmatched a row, whatever its a.k.

name: ne_eqi_select_swap_no_filter
left: SELECT a.k, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
right: SELECT b.k, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k
why: On an unmatched row a.k has a value and b.k is NULL.

name: ne_eqi_on_const_to_where
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND a.k = 2
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 2
why: A test on the preserved side in ON keeps the a row; in WHERE it drops it.

name: eqi_in_list_into_on
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k IN (1, 2)
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k IN (1, 2) WHERE a.k IN (1, 2)
why: A kept a row has a.k in (1, 2), so its matches have b.k in (1, 2).

name: ne_eqi_where_or
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.k = 2 OR a.x = 1
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k = 2 WHERE a.k = 2 OR a.x = 1
why: Under OR, a row kept by a.x = 1 may have a.k other than 2 and lose its match.

name: ne_eqi_other_column
left: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k WHERE a.x = 2
right: SELECT a.id, b.y FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.k = b.k AND b.k = 2 WHERE a.x = 2
why: a.x = 2 says nothing about b.k.
